Sapta Sindhava signifying the land of the seven rivers in the northwest - this concept's gloss. Already linked and correct.
The origin and meaning of Bharatavarsha, the country of the Bharatas, extending to the entire subcontinent - this concept's opening.
Ashoka using Jambudvipa for the whole of India, which then included Bangladesh, Pakistan and parts of Afghanistan - this concept's inscription evidence. Already linked and correct.
The Vishnu Purana defining Bharata as the country north of the ocean and south of the snowy mountains - this concept quotes that verse in Sanskrit and in translation.

Yintu also originally coming from Sindhu - this concept's opening sentence about the Chinese names.
Xuanzang's 7th century CE visit, 17 years in India, and the Buddhist texts he translated from Sanskrit into Chinese - this concept's box. Already linked and correct.
Hindustan coming into use, first in a Persian inscription some 1,800 years ago and later among most invaders of India. Already linked and correct.

The rivers of the subcontinent's plains are a question about the physical map of the Indian Subcontinent that this concept opens on and sends the reader back to; no other concept in the chapter treats the region as physical geography.
The northern boundary of the subcontinent - this concept's THINK ABOUT IT asks the reader to make out the natural boundaries on the map, and the Himalayas are named in the epigraph above it.

The role of ancient texts as sources for India's names - this concept states that the names come to us from ancient texts, accounts of travellers and pilgrims, and inscriptions, and then works from the oldest source available.

How foreign accounts contributed to India's nomenclature across Persians, Greeks and Chinese together is this concept's summary statement - foreign visitors to or invaders of India mostly adopted names derived from the Sindhu, which resulted in Hindu, Indoi and eventually India.

How India became the accepted international name - this concept's chain, Sindhu to Persian Hindu to Greek Indoi with the h dropped, is what it calls the reason the country carries that name in English today.

The king's domain in ancient Tamil literature, known from Cape Kumari in the south to the great mountain in the north and the oceans east and west - this concept quotes that poem and draws the conclusion about geographical knowledge.

Why inhabitants and foreigners name a region differently - this concept opens on India being called by many names both by its inhabitants and by visitors from outside, with inhabitants glossed as people who live in a particular place.
The Indus as the source of Hind, Hindu, Indoi and India - this concept is the mechanism, a foreign name for India being a foreign pronunciation of an Indian river.

The evolution of Bharata and Jambudvipa with textual and inscriptional evidence - this concept is where the literary terms are explained and then corroborated by Ashoka's inscription of about 250 BCE. Already linked and correct.
How foreigners derived their names from Sindhu and the linguistic transformations involved - Persian Hind, Hidu, Hindu and then Greek Indoi with the h dropped. Already linked and correct.
The statement being elaborated - the region has had many different names and shifting boundaries - is this concept's own sentence, and the question asks the reader to unpack it with examples.
How the Constitution reconciles the historical names by saying India, that is Bharat, and why that mattered - this concept's box. Already linked and correct.

The motivations of ancient travellers and how they shaped the naming of the land - this concept's closing question asks why people travelled to India and what their motivations could have been, and its summary sets Indian names against foreign ones.

The Himalayas and the surrounding oceans as the features that shape the concept and boundaries of the subcontinent - this concept's epigraph names the Himalayas and the two seas and its THINK ABOUT IT asks the reader to find them.
The Hindustan half of the comparison, its Persian origin from Sindhu and later use by invaders, is this concept's content. Already linked and defensible, so left alone.
How the absence of the h sound in Greek changed the name - this concept is where that phonetic loss between two foreign languages is said to have produced the modern English name.
The statement being justified, that ancient Indians knew their geography well, is this concept's own remark, made after the Vishnu Purana verse and the Tamil poem that describe the land's extent.
Tianzhu readable as heavenly master, reflecting the respect the ancient Chinese had for India as the land of the Buddha - this concept's point. Already linked and correct.

Why it matters that Hindu was geographical and not religious - this concept inserts exactly that caution, that in ancient Persian Hindu is a purely geographical term and does not refer to the Hindu religion.
The map of the regions the Mahabharata lists, from Kashmira to Kerala, and what their number implies - this concept's LET'S EXPLORE works from that map. Already linked and correct.

Persian merchants of the 6th century BCE speaking of Hidu and its mighty river, and Greek traders later saying Indoi - this concept dates the Persian campaign to the 6th century BCE and explains both names from Sindhu.

A Jambudvipa stretching from the northern mountains to the southern seas, dated to about 250 BCE, and the name's meaning from the jamun fruit - all of it is this concept's Ashoka material. Already linked and correct.
A citizen choosing Bharat on an official form, and where the Constitution mentions both names - this concept's DON'T MISS OUT box on India, that is Bharat. Already linked and correct.
A 7th century map of Xuanzang's routes, a name he would have recognised, and why India was the land of heavenly master - every sub-prompt comes from this concept. Already linked and correct.
